evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.213 (Lewis & Short): hunc ego appellō ōrātōrem
Liv. 1.15 (Lewis & Short): envoys sent to sue for peace
terms.comment: One who speaks in public, in court or before an assembly, and so the trained orator; in early Latin and Livy also an envoy who carries a spoken message (Lewis & Short). Not the person who happens to be talking.

evidence: Plaut. Curc. 229: Quis hic est quī loquitur?
terms.comment: Latin names the person by what they are doing: quī loquitur, the one talking; quī dīcit, the one making a speech. A speaker of Latin is quī Latīnē loquitur (see speak a language).

evidence: Apul. M. 1 (Lewis & Short): rudis locūtor exōticī sermōnis
terms.comment: Post-classical and rare: in Apuleius a speaker of a language, in Gellius a babbler (Lewis & Short). Use quī loquitur.
